9	# Write Simply
10	
11	> **Purpose:** `core/pattern-rules.md` says what to cut. This file says what to aim for, and how
12	> to tell when a draft got there. Loaded on every writing job, right after the pattern rules.
13	>
14	> Distilled from three Paul Graham essays: [Write Simply](https://paulgraham.com/simply.html),
15	> [Good Writing](https://paulgraham.com/goodwriting.html) and
16	> [Writes and Write-Nots](https://paulgraham.com/writes.html). The observations are his. The rules
17	> and the vault wiring are mine.
18	
19	## 1. Simple is the default, complex is a decision
20	
21	Use ordinary words and short sentences. Keep the technical term and simplify every word around it.
22	
23	A complicated sentence written on purpose is a tool. A complicated sentence written by accident is
24	clumsy. Both look the same on the page, so the writer is the only person who can tell them apart.
25	Never write one by accident.
26	
27	This rule also protects a draft. An edit that flattens a deliberate long sentence has broken
28	something, so read the intent before you cut.
29	
30	## 2. Every sentence spends the reader's energy
31	
32	A reader arrives with a fixed amount of attention. Energy spent on your prose is energy that never
33	reaches your idea.
34	
35	Most readers quit part way through a long piece. Lower friction means more of them finish. That is
36	the entire return on an hour of cutting.
37	
38	Fancy writing moves work onto the reader so the writer looks clever. Do not charge them for that.
39	
40	**What changed in 2026.** The reader now has a model open in the next tab. Ask it your question and
41	it answers in four sentences, with no warm-up and no history of the field. That is the piece your
42	draft competes against, and it costs the reader nothing to switch.
43	
44	So the price of a slow opening moved. It used to cost a little attention. It now costs the whole
45	reader, because the shorter version already exists and sits one keystroke away. The same holds for
46	a padded middle and for a term you left unexplained. A reader who has to guess stops guessing and
47	asks the model instead.
48	
49	Three faults are fatal now, in this order. The piece takes too long to reach its claim. The piece
50	buries the claim under qualifiers and clauses. The piece uses a word the reader does not have.
51	`SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py` checks all three: `slow-lede` for the first, `padded` for the second,
52	`undefined-term` for the third.
53	
54	What survives is the part a model cannot produce: the number you measured, the thing you tried that
55	failed, the decision you made and the reason. Write those first and cut toward them.
56	
57	## 3. A hard topic does not license hard words
58	
59	Many readers do not read English first. Their grasp of the idea often runs ahead of their grasp of
60	the language. Write plainly because the subject is hard. Difficulty never grants permission to stop.
61	
62	The same choice buys durability. A reader ten years from now sits in the same position as a foreign
63	reader today, because the language and the references will have moved.
64	
65	## 4. Plain prose is an honesty test
66	
67	Complicated writing hides missing ideas, and some writers pick it for that reason. Say nothing
68	simply and everyone sees it, including you.
69	
70	So when a sentence resists becoming plain, inspect the idea before you inspect the words. The
71	resistance is usually the idea, and no rewrite fixes an idea that is not there.
72	
73	## 5. A sentence that sounds wrong usually means the idea is wrong
74	
75	Prose that reads well is more likely to be right. The mechanism is simple. You will never rewrite
76	an awkward passage into a version you believe less, so any forced change moves toward what you
77	actually meant.
78	
79	State the claim in the safe direction. Good sound proves internal consistency rather than truth,
80	because a careful liar also sounds good. Read the signal the other way instead. A passage that
81	reads badly almost always carries a broken idea inside it.
82	
83	The diagnostic is one question. When a line reads badly, do not reach for a synonym. Ask what you
84	meant to say there.
85	
86	This holds for writing that develops an idea. It does not hold for a piece that reports finished
87	work, such as a release note or a build report, where the thinking already happened elsewhere.
88	
89	## 6. Two edits that improve a draft with no new thinking
90	
91	**Force a length change.** Take one paragraph and make it a line shorter. The constraint is
92	arbitrary and the result still improves, because a rewrite cannot move away from what you meant.
93	Use it on any paragraph you cannot fix by argument.
94	
95	**Read as the first reader.** The writer reads the draft more times than anybody else will. Read it
96	cold and mark every place where something catches. Then repair the idea at that spot, not the word.
97	
98	## 7. Rhythm follows the idea, never a meter
99	
100	Good rhythm is not regular. A simple idea gets a short sentence. A subtle idea needs a long one to
101	carry its conditions.
102	
103	An even cadence is therefore a defect, and so is a clipped sentence added for punch. Never
104	regularise a draft, and never truncate one.
105	
106	## 8. Writing is thinking, so keep the thinking
107	
108	Leslie Lamport put the stake plainly: "If you're thinking without writing, you only think you're
109	thinking."
110	
111	AI removed most of the pressure to write. The population now splits into writers and non-writers,
112	which is the same line as the split between thinkers and non-thinkers.
113	
114	This is the villain in [World](../World.md) wearing a new coat. Handing a draft to a model whole is
115	renting the thinking. Use a model to draft, to argue and to check. Keep every decision about what
116	the piece claims.
117	
118	## 9. The reader was not in the room
119	
120	Every term has a first appearance. That is the sentence where the reader either
121	keeps reading or starts guessing.
122	
123	Guessing costs more than stopping. A reader who stops looks the word up and
124	comes back right. A reader who guesses reads the next ten paragraphs against
125	the wrong definition and never finds out.
126	
127	Two kinds of word cause this, and only one of them is your problem to fix.
128	
129	**A borrowed term** is real industry vocabulary. `webhook`, `context window`,
130	`fine-tune`. A reader who searches for one gets the correct answer in a click.
131	Leave it bare and the reader takes one detour.
132	
133	**An owned term** is one this vault coined, or bent to a private meaning.
134	`harness`, `load order`, `state file`, `flywheel`, `second brain`,
135	`digital twin`, `ICP`. A reader who searches for one of these gets somebody
136	else's definition and walks away confidently wrong. The internet cannot rescue
137	that. Only your page can.
138	
139	So an owned term carries its meaning where it first appears. Four shapes do the
140	job, and the scorer accepts all four.
141	
142	| Shape | Example |
143	|---|---|
144	| Copula | a harness is everything you build around the model |
145	| Naming clause | a hook, which is a script that runs on its own |
146	| Parenthetical | the load order (the sequence those files arrive in) |
147	| Concepts table | `\| Harness \| Everything around the model \| You own this part \|` |
148	
149	For a piece that leans on four or more owned terms, put the concepts table
150	before the argument. Rule 10 in
151	[Long-Form Writing Rules](../Long-Form%20Writing%20Rules.md) already asks for
152	this on unfamiliar areas, and it costs the reader twenty seconds.
153	
154	Numbers break the same rule from the other side. A paragraph carrying four
155	separate figures hands the reader nothing to hold, so none of them land. Rule 4
156	of the same file asks for a number per claim. Four numbers in one breath is one
157	wall, not four claims.
158	
159	Run the check. `python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py "<file>"`, and CRIT reaches 0.
160	A hook blocks the write while it does not, because this is the rule a tired
161	writer skips first.
162	
163	**Where this came from.** On 2026-09-04 a batch of 49 pieces cleared slop CRIT 0,
164	LinkedIn format CRIT 0 and SEO 0, and a reader outside the meeting still could
165	not follow one of them. Every gate measured the words. None of them asked whether
166	the reader had been handed the words first.
167	
168	## 10. The pass
169	
170	Run this with the section 7 checklist in `core/pattern-rules.md`, after the scorer reaches CRIT 0.
171	
172	- [ ] Read one paragraph aloud. Does any sentence use a word a smart non-native reader would stop on?
173	- [ ] Find the most complicated sentence in the draft. Was it a decision, or an accident?
174	- [ ] Find the sentence that reads worst. Fix the idea under it rather than the wording.
175	- [ ] Take the weakest paragraph and cut it by one line. Keep the shorter version unless it lost a fact.
176	- [ ] Read the sentence lengths across one section. Is the cadence even enough to feel machine set?
177	- [ ] Name the decision in this piece that came from you and not from the model. If none exists, stop.
178	- [ ] List every owned term in the draft. Does each one carry its meaning where it first appears?
179	- [ ] Find the paragraph with the most figures in it. Can a reader hold all of them?
180	- [ ] Read the first 40 words alone. Do they carry a figure, a name, a command, or the reader?
181	- [ ] Ask what a model would answer in four sentences. Does your draft add anything past that?
182	
183	## Related
184	
185	- [Runtime contract](./runtime-contract.md), the load order and the checks
186	- [Pattern rules](./pattern-rules.md), the failure shapes a regex cannot catch
187	- [AI Writing Policy](../AI%20Writing%20Policy.md), the top directive
188	- [World](../World.md), the villain and the skill tree

197	
198	# Pattern Rules
199	
200	> **Purpose:** `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py` catches words. This file catches shapes. A draft can
201	> score CRIT 0 and still read like a machine wrote it, because the tell is the sentence structure
202	> and not the vocabulary. Loaded on every writing job, right after the runtime contract.
203	>
204	> Sections 1 to 4 say what to remove. Section 5 says what to leave alone, and it carries the same
205	> weight. Adapted from `core/anti-ai-rules.md` and `core/ai_slop_commandments.md` in
206	> [Deupaxx/EveryDay-Writer](https://github.com/Deupaxx/EveryDay-Writer). The mechanism notes are
207	> theirs. The wording and the thresholds are mine.
208	
209	Each rule below names the pattern, the mechanism that produces it, and the fix. The mechanism
210	matters. A rule you understand survives a rewrite, and a rule you memorised does not.
211	
212	## 1. Sentence shapes
213	
214	**The copula dodge.** A model replaces `is` with `serves as`, `stands as`, `represents`, `marks`,
215	`boasts`, `features` or `offers`. The mechanism is a repetition penalty. The model avoids reusing
216	the common word `is`, and the substitute implies a relationship that does not exist. Write `is`.
217	Keep `serves as` only where a real function sits beyond plain identity.
218	
219	**Tacked-on analysis.** A participle clause bolted to the end of a sentence to fake depth. The
220	shapes are `highlighting its importance`, `underscoring the shift`, `reflecting a broader trend`
221	and `marking a significant moment`. These clauses carry no new fact. They claim the fact before
222	them matters and supply no evidence. Cut the clause. If the significance is real, write it as its
223	own sentence with its own proof.
224	
225	**Unearned significance.** A claim of impact, legacy or scale with no support in the same
226	paragraph. Watch for `a pivotal moment`, `a key turning point`, `setting the stage for` and
227	`an enduring legacy`. Training data rewards important-sounding prose, so the
228	model asserts importance and expects the evidence to arrive later. State only what the evidence
229	carries. Real significance falls out of the evidence on its own.
230	
231	**The courtroom noun.** A judgment word standing in for a result nobody adjudicated. `verdict` is the
232	current one, and it arrives as `so the honest answer is not a verdict, it's a break-even calculation`
233	or as `the verdict is still out`. The same move hides in `ruling`, `the jury is out`, `case closed`,
234	`indictment` and `exonerates`. Two things break at once. The noun is a metaphor doing the work of a
235	number, and the `not a verdict, it's Y` frame negates a word the reader never proposed, which is the
236	banned antithesis with a straw man inside it. Write the result, the number, or the reason you cannot
237	tell yet. Keep the word where a real decision with named values exists, such as a court, or software
238	that emits one.
239	
240	**Vague authority.** A claim attributed to an unnamed group. `Experts agree`, `studies suggest`,
241	`research shows`, `observers note` and `industry reports indicate` all simulate a source. Name the
242	expert, link the study, or drop the claim. There is no third option.
243	
244	**The false range.** A `from X to Y` span where X and Y do not sit on one spectrum. The sentence
245	`From innovation to cultural change, AI is rewriting everything` reads as coverage and states
246	nothing. Name the two or three real things.
247	
248	**Name-dropping.** A list of outlets, tools or names with no fact attached. `Featured in Forbes,
249	TechCrunch and Wired` names sources and says nothing. The model lists authority to borrow it. Pick
250	one name and say what it said, or cut the list.
251	
252	**Abstract metaphor nouns.** A concrete idea dressed as a technical term. The set is `substrate`,
253	`vector` used for a way, `locus`, `vantage`, `nexus`, `bedrock`, `modality` and `endgame`. Each one
254	reads as precise and hides a plainer word: `base`, `way`, `place`, `last phase`. Pick the plain
255	word. His own working terms are exempt, because he chose them on purpose. `harness`, `flywheel`,
256	`scaffolding`, `surface` and `primitive` stay. The precedence ladder in the runtime contract
257	settles any other case, and it favours his voice.
258	
259	**The aphorism formula.** An ordinary claim dressed as reusable wisdom. The shapes are
260	`X is the currency of Y`, `the architecture of X` and `X becomes a trap`. This sounds
261	profound and loses the fact. Rule 23 in `slop_rules.py` bans the clever one-liner. This is the
262	same failure with a formula behind it, so replace the formula with the concrete claim under it.
263	
264	**The theatrical opener.** A standalone `Honestly?`, `Look,`, `Real talk` or `Here is the thing`
265	placed before an ordinary point. The tell is the fake reveal, because a person being honest just
266	says the thing. The same words mid-sentence in casual prose are ordinary English, so read the
267	position and not the word.
268	
269	**Adverbs propping up weak verbs.** `He ran very quickly` hides `he sprinted`. When the adverb is
270	load-bearing, the verb is wrong. Replace the verb and delete the adverb.
271	
272	**Elegant variation.** The model renames its subject to avoid repeating it, so one person becomes
273	`the researcher`, then `the prominent figure`, then `the key player`. Rule 28 says one word for one
274	thing. This is the mechanism it defends against. Repeat the real name.
275	
276	## 2. Paragraph and section shapes
277	
278	**False balance.** The three-step formula runs positive framing, then a nod at problems, then
279	instant dismissal. `Despite these challenges, the opportunity is enormous` is the shape of
280	analysis with none of the work. Engage the problem and let it stand, or drop the pretence.
281	
282	**Tricolon saturation.** The rule of three is a real device and a model reaches for it by default,
283	because three items look thorough with no need to be thorough. One tricolon per paragraph, never
284	two in a row. Four real items get listed as four. Two real items get written as prose.
285	
286	**The outline wrapper.** Section titles that a template chose rather than the content. The set is
287	`Challenges and future directions`, `Key takeaways`, `Legacy and impact`, `Overview` and
288	`Background`. Each one announces generation before a reader reads a word. Rule 4 in `Voice.md`
289	already demands a heading that states a conclusion, so name what the section delivers.
290	
291	**Fractal recapping.** A summary before a section starts, and another after it ends. Both
292	`In this section we will cover` and `as we have seen` are padding inherited from textbooks. Rule 15
293	bans the trailing summary, and this rule bans the leading one. Write forward.
294	
295	**Diff-anchored writing.** Prose that narrates a change instead of describing the thing. The line
296	`This section replaces the old onboarding flow` only makes sense to a reader who saw the old one. A
297	changelog, a release note and a migration guide are version-scoped by nature and are exempt.
298	Everything else reads coherently to a reader who arrived today.
299	
300	**One-point dilution.** The same claim restated ten times across four thousand words, sold as depth.
301	Say the claim once. Then spend the length on evidence, on the counterargument, and on what follows.
302	
303	**The undone claim.** A later line quietly reverses an earlier one. The hook promises a result and the
304	close hedges it. A post says "about thirty minutes" and its pinned comment says "under one hour". Each
305	line reads fine alone, so the writer is the least likely person to see it. Read line 1 against line 2,
306	line 2 against the body, the ending against the opening, and the pinned comment against the post. Fix
307	the weaker line and leave the stronger one. Never rewrite both.
308	
309	**The echo stack.** Three or more consecutive lines built on one skeleton, such as "The page lacks X.
310	There is no Y. Z does not exist." The model repeats the last structure it wrote, and a person
311	escalates. Make each line add a fact or raise the cost, keep the strongest, and put the rest in one
312	list whose items differ in shape. Swapping synonyms into the same skeleton keeps the echo.
313	
314	## 3. Fill that is not content
315	
316	**Assistant bleed.** The set is `I hope this helps`, `Certainly`, `Would you like me to`,
317	`Feel free to adjust` and `Here is a draft of`. Each one belongs in a chat window, and inside a
318	deliverable each one is contamination. Start with the content.
319	
320	**Cutoff disclaimers.** The set is `As of my last update`, `while specific details are limited`
321	and `based on available information`. Each one is a hedge formatted as content. Say the honest
322	thing once instead, or ask him.
323	
324	**Placeholder leakage.** An unfilled field that ships. `[insert link]`, `INSERT_SOURCE_URL`,
325	`access-date 2026-XX-XX` and `add image if available` all reach the reader when nobody re-read the
326	draft. A bracket from the fabrication rule is deliberate and stays visible on purpose. A bracket
327	from a template is a defect.
328	
329	**Promotional register.** The set is `nestled`, `in the heart of`, `vibrant`, `boasts`, `renowned`
330	and `a diverse array`. All of it comes from tourism copy and press releases. Write the neutral
331	declarative version instead.
332	Rule 8 in `Voice.md` says the same thing from the other side, so say what the thing does.
333	
334	## 4. Formatting tells
335	
336	**Em dash density.** Already CRIT in `slop_rules.py`, so this is the reason behind that ban. Model
337	output uses the em dash far above human rates and puts it where a comma belongs. Do not trade the em
338	dash for parentheses or an en dash. That move swaps one tell for another. End the sentence, or use a
339	comma.
340	
341	**The colon as a connector.** A colon that joins two clauses mid-sentence fakes a cause. The line
342	`The fix is simple: you rewrite the query` adds nothing that a period would not. A colon is correct
343	before a list or an example. Everywhere else, end the sentence. Rule 17 in `slop_rules.py` already
344	bans a colon in a heading, and this is the same tell inside a line.
345	
346	**Bold on every key phrase in running prose.** Emphasis stops meaning anything once it is
347	everywhere. Reserve bold for a term you are defining, or for a label that opens a line. Rule 2 in
348	`Voice.md` sets the boundary per folder. A bold label must earn its place with a new fact after it.
349	`**Performance:** Performance improved 40%` fails, because the label only repeats the line.
350	`**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file` passes, because the detail is new.
351	
352	**Sentence case in an H2.** Every H2 uses AP Title Case, in every channel, and states the claim
353	its section proves. `SCRIPTS/slop/heading_case.py` blocks a miscased H2 and flags a topic label.
354	H1 and H3 and below keep the case their destination uses. A model that capitalises every word of
355	an H3 or a body label is still showing the old tell.
356	
357	**A skipped heading level, or a rule above every heading.** Jumping H2 to H4, or dropping `---`
358	before each section by reflex, are both template tics. Neither is a writing choice.
359	
360	## 5. What to leave alone
361	
362	Sections 1 to 4 are a list of things to remove. Applied without judgement they produce the second
363	failure, which is prose stripped so hard that nobody is home. That output is not human. It is a
364	different machine's output, and it is the source of every complaint that edited writing reads flat,
365	boring and sanded down.
366	
367	**None of the following is evidence of AI on its own.** Do not cut one unless it sits in a cluster
368	with real tells.
369	
370	- Clean grammar and a consistent style. Many writers are edited. Polish proves nothing.
371	- Formal vocabulary. The banned list names specific overused words. It does not ban intelligence.
372	  Leave "ostensibly", "notwithstanding" and "constituent" where they are the right word.
373	- A mix of casual and formal register. That usually marks a technical writer, not a chatbot.
374	- Dry, plain prose. For a runbook it is correct.
375	- One transition word. A single "however" is English. The pile-up is the tell.
376	- One short emphatic sentence. People land points with a clipped sentence. Flag the drumbeat only
377	  when several stack up and inflate the tone.
378	- A salutation or a sign-off. Letters are older than chatbots.
379	- An unsourced claim. Most writing is unsourced. That is a rigor problem and not an AI problem.
380	- A watched word inside a quotation, a title, a proper noun or an example. When the piece discusses
381	  the phrase rather than uses it, leave it exactly as written.
382	
383	## 6. What to protect
384	
385	Removing tells is half the job. The other half is leaving alive whatever was already alive. These
386	are the hardest things for a model to produce and the easiest for an eager edit to erase.
387	
388	- **Odd, specific, hard-to-invent detail.** A real address. A strange quote. "The lawyer who worked
389	  upstairs from my dentist." Models round specifics off and people hoard them. Never generalise one
390	  of these to make a sentence flow.
391	- **Mixed feelings left unresolved.** "I think this is mostly right and it still bothers me." A
392	  model defaults to a clean take. Do not resolve the tension for him.
393	- **Dated references.** Slang, a meme, an in-joke anchored to one year and one subculture. Models
394	  lag by a year, so these are strong human signal.
395	- **A genuine aside or a self-correction.** A parenthesis where the writer interrupts himself.
396	  Machines rarely do that.
397	- **Uneven rhythm.** A nine-word sentence next to a forty-word one. Model output drifts toward one
398	  uniform mid-length cadence. The variance is the signal, so never regularise it.
399	- **An opinion he can defend.** If he can say why he chose a word, that reasoning outranks every
400	  rule in this file.
401	- **A deliberate quirk.** A writer who always opens lowercase, or never uses a semicolon, is doing
402	  something. Match it.
403	
404	**The operating principle is clusters, not instances.** One em dash means nothing. An em dash plus
405	a tricolon plus "vibrant tapestry" plus a "Challenges" heading is a confession.
406	
407	When you cannot tell whether something is his voice or a machine default, the precedence ladder in
408	the runtime contract decides it. Assume it is his, and leave it.
409	
410	**When a draft carries none of the signals in section 6, the problem is not that AI patterns
411	remain.** The problem is that nobody is home. Adding a specific, a stance and some unevenness beats
412	deleting one more banned word. The fabrication rule sets the limit on how a specific gets added.
413	It comes from him, never from invention.
414	
415	## 7. The pass before you hand it over
416	
417	Run this after the scorer reaches CRIT 0, because the scorer cannot see any of it.
418	
419	- [ ] Any "serves as" or "represents a" standing in for "is"?
420	- [ ] Any tacked-on participle claiming significance?
421	- [ ] Any impact claim with no evidence beside it?
422	- [ ] Any unnamed authority carrying a fact?
423	- [ ] Two tricolons in a row, or a tricolon that hides four real items?
424	- [ ] A template heading, a leading recap, or a trailing recap?
425	- [ ] Any assistant bleed, cutoff hedge or leftover placeholder?
426	- [ ] Any colon joining two clauses where a period belongs?
427	- [ ] Any bold label that only repeats the line after it?
428	- [ ] Any metaphor noun where a plain word fits, outside his working terms?
429	- [ ] Any list of names or outlets with no fact attached?
430	- [ ] Any fact, name, number or source that he did not supply?
431	- [ ] Does any later line undo an earlier one? Read the hook against line 2, the body against the pinned comment, and the ending against the opening.
432	- [ ] Cover everything after the opening. Can you still guess how the piece ends? If so, the hook answered itself.
433	- [ ] Did anything from section 5 get cut that should have stayed?
434	- [ ] Did every signal in section 6 survive the edit?
435	- [ ] List every heading in the draft on one line. Does any heading state an outline slot rather than a claim, so it would sit unchanged over a different topic?
436	- [ ] Find the one sentence in the draft that only Atharva could have written: a real date, a named person, a number from his own work, a moment he was wrong. If no such sentence exists, the draft is not done.
437	- [ ] If the piece covers several parallel items, read only the closing line of each one in a row. Do they all sound interchangeable with the nouns swapped?
438	
439	## 7b. Fixing a MED without creating the next one
440	
441	Each advisory the scorer raises has one right fix. The other fix costs four to six rounds of
442	edit-and-rescore, and that is where most of the time on a clean draft goes.
443	
444	**`readability-fragment` and `readability-bullet-fragment`: add a finite verb, never merge.**
445	"Speed multiplier." becomes "A speed multiplier finishes their own tasks faster." Do not fold
446	the fragment into the sentence before it. Measured across `2_PUBLISHED` and `1_DRAFTS` on
447	2026-08-29: adding a verb created a new `ste-long-sentence` hit in 0 of 239 paragraphs, and
448	merging created one in 6. A fragment caps at nine words and a long sentence starts at
449	twenty-one, so a verb cannot cross the gap. A merge can.
450	
451	**`repeated-consecutive-opener`: escalate, do not reword.** Three lines that open on the same word
452	are an echo stack (section 2). Keep the strongest line, make each other line add a fact or raise the
453	cost, or fold the weak ones into one list whose items differ in shape.
454	
455	**`ste-long-sentence`: split at the clause, and check the halves.** Halving a 45-word
456	sentence leaves two 22-word sentences, both still over. Cut to the real clause boundary
457	instead, or drop a subordinate clause outright.
458	
459	**`ste-progressive` and `ste-perfect`: change the tense, do not restructure.** "They were
460	publishing videos" becomes "They published videos". A rewrite around the verb pulls a
461	fragment or a long sentence in behind it.
462	
463	**`readability-long-paragraph`: cut a sentence, do not join two.** Joining two sentences to
464	lower the count is the move that produces a long sentence. The scorer now only raises this
465	when the paragraph still holds a sentence over 20 words, so splitting one is always safe.
466	
467	## 8. Corpus-level shapes
468	
469	Sections 1 to 4 catch a tell inside one sentence or one paragraph. These four hide at the
470	scale of the whole piece, or across many pieces, so a single-file read misses them. The 2026-08-28
471	audit of all 78 published articles found each one repeating across most of the corpus, on
472	unrelated topics, which is what told a reader the pattern was the machine and not the writer.
473	Full findings: [AI Slop Reader Audit, 2026-08-28](../../INBOX/Reports/AI-Slop-Reader-Audit-2026-08-28.md).
474	
475	**The generic macro-skeleton.** Hook, why-it-matters, a numbered list or a run of parallel
476	sections, a recap, a closing call to action. A reader who has read enough AI explainers
477	recognizes this shape before evaluating a single claim in it, because the same headings
478	("Why This Matters", "Key Takeaways", "The Bigger Takeaway", "Wrapping Up", "Who This Is For")
479	would sit unchanged over almost any other topic. A heading must name the specific claim inside
480	its section, not the outline slot it fills. Found in roughly 83% of the audited corpus.
481	
482	**Zero first-person specificity.** Strip the byline and the piece runs unchanged on any other
483	blog covering the same topic, because every example is a generic hypothetical "you" or an
484	unnamed archetype rather than a named person, a real date, a real number from his own work, or
485	a moment he was wrong or surprised. This is the concrete thing a "reads AI" complaint detects,
486	even when the reader cannot name a rule. Every piece needs at least one detail only Atharva
487	could supply, woven into the opening or the close, not bolted on as an afterthought paragraph.
488	Found in roughly 64% of the audited corpus, the single most common reason cited.
489	
490	**Per-item template stamping.** When a piece covers several parallel items (tools, films,
491	terms, chapters, entries in a series), every item runs through the identical clause-by-clause
492	mold: same heading shape, same bolded lead-in, same closing "lesson" sentence. A reader can
493	predict item 4 after reading item 2, which reads as one template with new nouns dropped in
494	rather than several separate acts of thinking. Vary structure across items on purpose: let
495	length, opening move, and closing move differ per entry so no two are interchangeable with the
496	nouns swapped. Concentrated in, but not limited to, multi-part series (Film School in Scenes,
497	Slaying Your 20s, the Uketsu deep dives) and long enumerations (a glossary, a tool roundup).
498	
499	**Announcing significance instead of demonstrating it.** Stock transition phrases that promise
500	weight the next sentence has not earned yet: "Here's the thing", "Here is what matters", "Let
501	me explain", "Here's the part most people miss". Stacking two or three of these in one short
502	piece reads as connective filler standing in for an actual transition. Delete the announcing
503	sentence and let the next sentence open the paragraph directly. If the paragraph reads weaker
504	without the announcement, the claim itself is not strong enough yet, so rewrite the claim
505	rather than propping it up with a preamble.
506	
507	A fifth shape from the same audit is not new prose to avoid, it is a gap in the mechanical
508	scorer: "X is not Y. It is Z." across two full sentences performs the exact negate-then-reveal
509	move that `ANTITHESIS_PATTERNS` in `slop_rules.py` already bans when it is joined by a comma,
510	and slips past untouched because the scorer checks one sentence at a time. Treat it as banned
511	under the same rule until the detector is extended to match across a sentence boundary.
512	
513	## 9. The Wikipedia cross-check, 2026-08-28
514	
515	Atharva ran [Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing)
516	plus a companion 38-badge detector list against this file. Most of the 38 were already covered by
517	a rule above under different wording (not-only-but-also, it's-important-to-note, testament,
518	crucial role, the ever-evolving landscape, the challenges-and-outlook formula, the tacked-on
519	participle, promotional boilerplate, chatbot leftovers). The genuine gaps are now mechanically
520	enforced in `slop_rules.py` and `score.py` rather than restated here, see `TIC_PATTERNS`,
521	`HARD_PHRASES`, and the stacked-questions and echoing-sentences checks in `score.py` for the
522	mechanism and the exact strings. Do not copy that list into this file, it would drift.
523	
524	A second pass on the same day built a probe file with one example sentence per badge and ran the
525	scorer over it. That probe found 20 of the 38 still silent, so the first pass had missed more than
526	it claimed. The 20 landed as 9 new regex shapes in `TIC_PATTERNS`, 4 advisory shapes in the new
527	`TIC_PATTERNS_SOFT`, a `repeated-consecutive-opener` run check in `score.py`, and about 50 new
528	fixed strings in `HARD_PHRASES` and `SOFT_PHRASES`. A backtest over 607 files across the vault, the
529	website and the marketing repo fired the new CRIT rules 35 times in total, and every hit read as a
530	real tic. Four dev-blog strings ("sane defaults", "zero config", "zero-config", "batteries
531	included") were demoted to SOFT in that backtest, because Airflow `default_args` advice and a
532	release note for a cache store both used them literally and correctly.
533	
534	Two writer-facing gaps closed with them. `rules_prompt.py` never rendered the tics, so the gate
535	blocked shapes the generated block in `CLAUDE.md` never named, and the banned headings had the same
536	problem. Both now render, and `TIC_DESCRIPTIONS` in `slop_rules.py` carries the plain-English form
537	of every tic. `rules_prompt.py` exits with an error when a tic has no description, so a new regex
538	cannot ship invisible to the writer.
539	
540	One item was deliberately left out. The source list flags a colon opening onto three or more
541	items ("separate ports, processes, and local state") and says so itself: noisy in technical
542	writing, off by default for a documentation corpus. Section 4 already states the opposite case as
543	correct here ("A colon is correct before a list or an example"), and this vault's own prose uses
544	that construction constantly and on purpose. Banning it would fail correct writing, so it stays a
545	human judgement call, not a scorer rule.
546	
547	## Related
548	
549	- [Runtime contract](./runtime-contract.md), the load order and the checks
550	- [AI Writing Policy](../AI%20Writing%20Policy.md), the top directive
551	- [Voice](../Voice.md), how the writing sounds
552	- [Technical Writing Style Guide](../Technical%20Writing%20Style%20Guide.md), the technical layer

content.content:
---
name: banger-tweets
description: Create engaging X (Twitter) posts that drive engagement and grow audience. Use this skill when asked to write X/Twitter content, craft viral tweets, or help with X engagement strategy. Triggers include requests for tweets, X posts, or social media content for X. Atharva is on X Premium+, so one post carries up to 25,000 characters and threads are retired.
---

# Writing X Posts

## Gate. Do these five things before you draft a single tweet

This applies to every request, including a one-line lazy prompt like "tweets about this". A short prompt does not mean a short procedure.

1. **Load the chain.** `DIGITAL TWIN/core/runtime-contract.md`, then
   `DIGITAL TWIN/core/pattern-rules.md`, then `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`, then `DIGITAL TWIN/Voice.md`, then this file. Nothing else
   loads for a tweet. Render the load-order (the sequence rule files load in) panel with `python SCRIPTS/loadorder/block.py --skill banger-tweets --file "<path>" --node "<node>" --topic "<the idea>"`. It looks the chain up itself and runs every scorer that applies, so the checks half is measured rather than typed. `--glob` takes a batch.
2. **Check for a matching Substack Note.** Run `python SCRIPTS/socials/parity.py --file "<the tweet
   file>"`. It pairs on `series` plus `sequence` first, then `source_blog`, then the title. When it
   names a Note, that Note is the material and the source article is not. Copy every number and
   claim across, then rewrite in the register below. See the parity rule in `SOCIALS/README.md`.
3. **Read `references/examples.md` in full.** It is not optional background. It is the calibration, and a draft written without it comes out as a summary instead of a tweet. If you skipped it, you are about to write the bad version. Part 1 holds real tweets from writers Atharva reads, each with the mechanic named, and it sets the bar. Part 2 holds the same shapes in his voice, and it sets the register. Read Part 1 first.
4. **Write the take for each tweet before you write the tweet.** One sentence, stating something Atharva believes and would defend. If you cannot state it, you do not have a tweet, you have a fact. Then name the take's box from `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`. Only box 4 becomes a tweet: non-obvious and usable today.
   Then run the opening gate in `LIBRARY/Resources/Post Uniqueness Check.md` on the first line. A tweet whose best fact sits in its last line moves that fact to the top.
5. **Never restate a banned word here.** The lists live in `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py` and reach you
   through `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. The shapes a regex cannot catch live in `core/pattern-rules.md`.

Then output this table before any drafts. It is short on purpose and it exists so the work is visible and checkable.

| # | Take (what he believes) | Box (net new value) | Shape | Evidence backing it |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Never skip the table. It is the difference between drafting and reporting.

## When a tweet will not start, borrow a winning shape

[Swipefile](https://swipefile.com/) holds about 14,000 tagged examples that already worked, including 903 social and X posts, 3,214 copywriting entries and 2,433 advice entries. Each one carries a short teardown of why it worked. Use [swipefile.com/category/social](https://swipefile.com/category/social) for X specifically.

Borrow the shape, never the words. The take stays Atharva's and the evidence stays his. A swiped hook with his claim under it is a tweet. A swiped hook with a swiped claim is theft and it reads like someone else.

Read the full entry in `LIBRARY/Lists/tools and software directory.md`.

## The one rule that fixes 90% of bad tweets

**The claim leads. The evidence backs it up.**

A tweet that opens by naming a company, a study, a person, or a report has already failed, because the subject of the sentence becomes "someone did research" instead of "here is what is true".

Mechanical test, run it on every draft: **read only the first six words.** If those words name a source, rewrite so the first six words say what you believe.

```
broken:  SparkToro measured their own accounts and found posts with links reach 10x fewer people.
fixed:   a post with a link reaches 10x fewer people than the same post without one. meta wrote
         that advice into their own help docs. they're not hiding the toll booth. you keep paying it.
```

Same fact. The first is a press release. The second costs the reader something.

When you are handed raw material (an article, a blog, a situation), find the sharpest uncomfortable truth inside it. That single sentence is the tweet. Everything else is packaging.

> **Where the angle comes from.** Pick the subject and argument shape from `LIBRARY/Resources/LinkedIn Content Formats - 100 Post Ideas.md`, top 10 first. That file never chooses the wording. Everything below governs how the tweet reads, and a tweet that sounds like a LinkedIn post has failed no matter which format it came from.

## No links in the post

An X post carries no URL. Not to the blog, not to a repository, not to a tool. X cuts the reach of a post that sends the reader off the platform, and Atharva pays that toll on every scheduled post.

This binds hardest on anything going out through Zernio, because those post on a schedule with nobody watching the numbers. Write the post so it stands alone and pays the reader on X.

Three ways to keep the value without the link.

**Name the thing.** "the glossary" and "pocketflow" cost nothing and a reader who wants it can search.

**Give the substance away.** The post carries the number, the rule or the step. A reader who wants the rest goes looking without being told to.

**End on the claim.** A post that ends on a URL taught the reader that the post was an advertisement. End on the sentence that was worth reading.

Never replace a link with "link in bio", "link in the replies", or "DM me for it". Those are the same toll with extra steps.

## One post, never a thread

Atharva is on X Premium+. One post holds up to 25,000 characters, so the reason threads existed is gone. Three rules follow from that and none of them bends.

**Never number a post.** No `1/`, no `2/`, no `🧵`, no "a thread". A point that needed three numbered parts is one post that runs longer.

**Never write a pinned comment.** The pinned first comment is a LinkedIn mechanic and it belongs to `write-linkedin-posts` alone. On X the link goes in the post body.

**Never split one argument across posts.** If part two only makes sense after part one, they are one post.

A file may still hold several posts separated by `---`, and that is a batch of independent posts, never a sequence. Each one stands alone and the reader can meet them in any order. A post regenerated from a Substack Note is the exception: that file holds exactly one post, because the pairing is one to one.

Length is a reach decision, not a rule. Short travels further, so stay short by default. Run long when the material is a system dump, or when the post carries its matching Note in full. Count the characters against 25,000 rather than estimating.

## Shapes. Pick one per tweet, never blend, rotate across a set

A set of 15 tweets that all use the same shape is one tweet written 15 times. Rotate deliberately. You cannot write a greentext about a study, which is the point: the shape forces different thinking.

**One-liner / nuke.** One sentence, no context, complete on its own.
`your CI pipeline being green doesn't mean the code works`

**Deadpan.** States something absurd like everyone already knows it. The flat delivery is the joke.
`running the same claude opus prompt 8 times because "maybe this time"`

**Staircase.** Lines get shorter, weight falls on the last one. White space does the work.
```
1,000 google searches
415 produce a click
360 land on a site google doesn't own

that's the open web's entire share
```

**Reverse pyramid.** Wide, then narrow, then one line that implodes.

**Greentext.** `>` lines, sequential, self-deprecating, ends `>mfw`. For things that went wrong. Write the arrow as a literal `>`, never as `>`, because the scorer reads the entity's semicolon as a banned semicolon and fails the file on one CRIT per line.
```
>read that video outperforms
>buy a camera
>learn premiere
>post to linkedin
>reaches 10x fewer people than plain text
>mfw
```

**Fragment.** Trails off. Lets the reader finish it.
`prompt caching exists and you're just...`

**Cocky take.** No hedging, no "in my experience". States it confidently. Invites the quote-tweet disagreement, which is free distribution.
`if your AI output sounds generic you gave it nothing. the model is fine. you are the problem.`

**Dry flex.** An achievement stated so flatly the lack of celebration is the flex.

**Shower thought.** Sounds offhand, cuts deep, makes people stop.
`"direct traffic" is your analytics tool saying "i don't know."`

**Story beat.** One real specific moment. No lesson attached to the end.

**Heuristic.** Name the trigger, name the correction, give the direction. The reader can run it tomorrow. Strongest shape in the mined corpus, so reach for it more than you think.

**Field note.** One mundane place or moment used as a sensor for a large trend. Dated, specific, and it stops before the lesson.

**Timestamped contrast.** Two dates, two lines, no commentary. `2008: build an app / 2023: build an app store`

**Dialogue.** A short transcript where the contradiction accuses the subject for you. One calm line of commentary after, at most.

**System dump.** The long post that lists a real working setup step by step. Every step names a tool and a trigger, every number is real, and it never closes on "comment X and I'll DM you". The shape most likely to run long, since X Premium+ now carries that length in the post itself.

Match shape to energy: hurts because true → one-liner or shower thought. Embarrassing → greentext or story beat. Can't believe it works this way → deadpan or fragment. Stating it without apology → cocky take. The visual has to land → staircase or pyramid.

## Voice

Lowercase reads casual and confident. Fragments are fine when the meaning is clear. No hedging, no "in my experience", no "this is just me". Specificity beats generality every time, so write "4 years" and "$340", never "a long time" and "a lot". Dark humor is fair game and self-deprecation earns trust. Silence the editor that wants to explain the joke.

## Hard bans

**Hook shapes:** "Unpopular opinion:", "Hot take:", "Nobody talks about this", "I used to think X. I was wrong.", "Steal this", "[Year] taught me [lesson]", "Here's what I learned:", "A thread 🧵". Also never open on a question, per Voice.md.

**Thread furniture:** `1/`, `2/`, `🧵`, "thread below", "more in the replies", and any pinned-comment line. All four are retired, see the one-post rule above.

**Closers:** "What do you think?", "Drop your thoughts below", "Tag someone who needs this", "Follow me for more", "Retweet if you agree", "Save this".

**Constructions:** the banned words, the negative parallelism forms and the tricolon cap are all in `slop_rules.py`, already in context. The copula dodge and the other shapes sit in section 1 of `core/pattern-rules.md`. Do not restate either list here, and do not treat the absence of a restatement as permission.

**AI tells specific to X:** perfect symmetry between setup and payoff, every tweet ending on a lesson, a clean three-act structure inside one tweet, explaining the joke in the last line. None of these four is in the scorer, so they are checked by reading.

## The judge pass. Score your own drafts before he sees them

Run this after the drafts exist and before the six mechanical checks. Score every tweet out of 5 on each axis, print the table, and rewrite anything below 18. Judging your own work feels redundant and it is the step that catches the three failures a read-through never does.

| Axis | 5 looks like | 1 looks like |
|---|---|---|
| Claim | He would defend this in a reply thread | A fact with no position on it |
| Specificity | Names, numbers, exact strings | "the best people", "a lot", "recently" |
| Register | Sounds like him out loud | Sounds like a caption |
| Standalone | Works with every other tweet covered | Needs the set to make sense |
| Shape fidelity | Matches the shape's real mechanic | Wears the shape's label only |

Three failure modes score low every time, so hunt them by name.

**The vague superlative.** "the four sharpest people i read", "one of the best threads", "a huge corpus". You have the names and the numbers in the material you were handed, so put them in. @nabeelqu's heuristic works because it quotes the exact sentence that triggers it. Any superlative without a name attached is an unfinished draft.

**Rhythm beating accuracy.** A line that scans better than the truth. Merging two tools into one, rounding a cost up, saying "paid" about something free. Every factual claim traces back to something that actually happened, and the version that scans worse ships.

**The borrowed line as payload.** Quoting someone else's sentence and letting it carry the tweet. The reader remembers them, not him. Quote someone only when your own take is the larger half, and never as the closing line.

## Before you hand it over

Run all nine. A failure on any one means rewrite, not ship.

1. **First six words of every tweet.** Any that name a source get rewritten.
2. **Shape rotation.** No two consecutive tweets share a shape, and no set leans on one shape.
3. **Negative parallelism scan.** Search every draft for the word "not" and for "isn't". Any tweet built as `X. not Y.` or as `this is not X, it is Y` gets rewritten to say Y on its own. This is the single most common construction that survives a first draft, so scan for it by hand rather than trusting a read-through.
4. **Character count.** The ceiling is 25,000 characters, not 280, because Atharva is on X Premium+. Count characters, do not estimate. Most posts still stay short, because a short post reads better and travels further.
5. **Thread scan.** Search every draft for `1/`, for `🧵`, and for the word "thread". Any hit is a rewrite into one post. Search for "pinned" as well, because that mechanic belongs to LinkedIn.
   **Link scan.** Search for `http`. Any hit comes out, including a link to his own blog. Search for "link in" too.
6. **Standalone check.** Cover every other post in the file. Does this one still work alone?
7. **Scorer.** `python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"` and CRIT must reach 0. Ignore the flow, paragraph and fragment findings, which are long-form rules that do not apply to short-form.

Run `python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py "<file>"` as well, and take CRIT to 0. It asks whether a reader outside this vault can follow the piece. Every CRIT names a term coined here, so searching the web gives the reader the wrong meaning and only a gloss on the page fixes it. A PostToolUse hook blocks the write while a CRIT stands.
8. **Pattern rules.** Section 7 of `core/pattern-rules.md`, run after the scorer. Then section 6 of the same file, because a set of tweets edited flat is worse than a set with one tell left in it.
9. **Uniqueness.** `LIBRARY/Resources/Post Uniqueness Check.md`, five questions. A tweet that fails question 1 (his frame, not just the fact) or question 5 (would any other account post this) does not ship.

## Output order

Show the take table, then the drafts, then the judge table with the rewrites already applied. Hand him the scored set rather than a first pass, because a draft he has to grade himself is work you moved onto his desk.

## Where the file goes

Check for an existing placeholder before writing anything. One file per topic per channel, never duplicate, never write outside `SOCIALS/Tweets/`.

Look for `SOCIALS/Tweets/tweet_[Exact Blog Title].md`. If it exists, write into it. If it does not, create it.

```markdown
---
type: Tweet
title: Exact Blog Title
source_blog: "[[Exact Blog Title]]"
description: "The hook, one line"
created: YYYY-MM-DD
updated: YYYY-MM-DD
posted: false
---

[the post, immediately, nothing between it and the frontmatter]
```

A post regenerated from a Substack Note carries `series` and `sequence` copied from that Note, because those two fields are what pair the file to it.

Use `source_blog: none` for original content with no source article. Never emit a `#tweet` tag and never emit a `**Source Blog:**` line, both retired 2026-07-27. Never put an extra `---` between the frontmatter and the post, because a stray one reads as a block break.

One file usually holds one post. A batch file may hold several independent posts separated by `---` on its own line, and the review desk shows each as its own card. Never number them, because they are not a sequence. A file paired to a Note holds exactly one post.

## Output

Show the take table, then the tweets. Add one line on why a shape fits only where it is genuinely interesting. Skip emoji headers, skip a "WHY THIS WORKS" section, skip the recap.

# FirstRun Marketing Plan

Marketing earns points in three places:

- **Building in public:** 15% of the score.
- **The demo video:** 20% of the score.
- **The community award:** $500 cash, which stacks with a top-3 place.

The community award looks at "genuine engagement" and "whether people are excited enough to try, share or talk about it". Follower count does not decide it. So the plan puts people's own docs into the product, instead of chasing likes.

## Four Rules Protect the Entry

1. **Tag `#neatHack` on every post.** Your Voice file bans hashtags. This one tag is the single exception, because the judges search for it.
2. **No bought engagement and no engagement pods.** Bots or bought likes disqualify the team.
3. **X build posts carry no link in the post body.** Put the repo link in the first reply. The submission post on Monday is the exception, because it must carry the repo and the demo.
4. **Never mock a team whose quickstart broke.** Open the issue or PR first, then post. Credit them when they fix it.

## The Core Mechanic Turns Readers Into Test Cases

From Sunday, posts end with: "Reply with your quickstart URL. FirstRun runs it and I reply with the result."

- Each reply is a person who tried the product, which is the strongest signal for the community award.
- Each result you reply with is a public, real run.
- Run only what people send. Report exactly what happened.
- Cap it at what you can run. Write "first 20 URLs" if replies pile up.

## Phase 0, Thu to Fri: Set the Stage

| # | Action | Time |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Add one line to your X bio and LinkedIn headline: "Building FirstRun at #neatHack". | 5 min |
| 2 | Follow on X: @neatlogs, the Entire account, the cfo.ai account, and the 5 judges. Turn on notifications for @neatlogs, so you see the submission post the moment it goes live. | 10 min |
| 3 | Check the exact X handles of Entire, cfo.ai and TheVibeFounder, and write them into the tag map below. | 10 min |
| 4 | Send the 5 judge connection notes from `02 Judges and Mentors.md`. | 15 min |
| 5 | Introduce yourself in the neatHack Discord: one line on who you are, one line on FirstRun, one question. | 5 min |
| 6 | Post 1 on X and LinkedIn with asset 3 from `11 Asset Manifest.md`. | 20 min |

## Phase 1, Sat to Sun: Post What Happens, as It Happens

| Post | When | Channel | Hook idea | Asset |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | Sat ~6 PM | X | The first trace: "Here is what an agent sees when it reads your docs." | Asset 6 |
| 3 | Sat ~10 PM | X + Substack Note | v1 failed in public: the 3 mistakes the agent made | Asset 7 |
| 4 | Sun ~7 PM | X + LinkedIn | The before and after numbers | Asset 8 |
| 5 | Sun night | X | A real quickstart that broke, and the PR | Asset 9 |

**A 20-minute engagement routine, twice a day:**

1. Search X for `#neatHack`. Reply with substance to 5 other builders' posts, such as a question about their approach or a trace tip that helped you.
2. Answer every reply on your own posts within 2 hours.
3. Share each post once in the Discord channel meant for showcases. One share per post, never more.
4. Comment on a judge's post only when you add a fact. Never comment to be seen.

## Phase 2, Mon Oct 12: Launch in a Fixed Order

| Time (IST) | Action |
|---|---|
| 6:30 PM | Quote text ready in a note: team, name, project, public repo, demo link |
| **7:00 to 7:05 PM** | **Submission quote post on X** (rule F4) |
| 7:10 PM | First reply under your own post: the 3-line summary and the numbers |
| 7:30 PM | LinkedIn launch post with asset 13 and the video uploaded natively |
| 8:00 PM | Discord showcase post with the X link |
| 8:30 PM | Substack Note with the video |
| 8:30 to 11:00 PM | Reply to every comment. Run every quickstart URL people send. |

## Phase 3, Tue Oct 13 to Fri Oct 16: Keep the Story Moving

Judging takes 4 days, and community interest keeps counting during that time.

# neatHack Build Log: FirstRun

## Project

- **Name:** FirstRun
- **Purpose:** FirstRun runs your quickstart in a clean container, finds the first step that breaks, and proves the fix with a second clean run.
- **Problem:** Quickstarts break when a package is renamed, a flag is removed or a version moves. Nobody on the team gets an alert. The first person who finds the break is a new user, and most new users leave.

## Team

- Atharva Shah ([@HighnessAtharva](https://github.com/HighnessAtharva)), solo.

## Stack

| Part | Tool |
|---|---|
| Language | Python 3.11 |
| Agent | Claude Agent SDK, model `claude-sonnet-5-5` at medium effort, auth through `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` |
| Tracing | neatlogs Python SDK 1.4.26, neatlogs CLI 0.2.0 |
| Sandbox | Docker Engine 29.8.2 in WSL Ubuntu 22.04, one fresh container per run |
| Docs reader | Firecrawl CLI 1.25.3 |
| Failure classifier | Jev (TypeSafe System One) |
| Session capture | Entire CLI 0.11.4: Checkpoints, Graph, Brain, Trails |
| Business plan | cfo.ai |

## Planning Happened Before the Event

Planning and tool tests happened before the event in a private repo. No FirstRun code was written before kickoff (Sat 2026-10-10, 12:30 PM IST).

## Build Log

### 2026-10-10 (Saturday)

- **12:30 to 13:10 IST.** Created the public repo, ran `entire enable --agent claude-code --search-skill --agent-help-skill` before commit 1, and pushed the Entire config, 6 Trail runners, and the Graph and Brain agent instructions.
- **13:20 IST.** Preflight passed: 4 keys present (lengths only checked), Docker 29.8.2 in WSL, `gh`, Firecrawl 1.25.3, Entire 0.11.4, the venv on Python 3.11. `entire doctor` reports no problems.
- **13:30 IST.** Scaffold: `pyproject.toml`, `src/firstrun/config.py` (the only file that names a model), `src/firstrun/tracing.py`.
  - `python -m neatlogs doctor --probe` passed 8 of 8 checks, including `TRACE_VISIBLE` and `TRACE_FINALIZED`.
  - The first FirstRun trace, `firstrun.hello`, is trace `fdcab847f3129a251c6ae45f00c76a1c`. It is finalized with 2 spans and tag `hello`, and the neatlogs CLI read it back.

Entire state at the scaffold commit, run by the build agent:

```text
$ entire status
● Enabled · branch main
  Agents · Claude Code
  Checkpoints sync to: origin
1 session

$ entire checkpoint list
  branch       main
  checkpoints  0
No checkpoints found on this branch.
```

The checkpoint count is 0 because the scaffold commit is the first commit made inside an agent session. Later entries record the count after it.

- **12:55 IST. Entire checkpoints hung on Git 2.33.** The post-commit hook waited 206 s on `git update-ref --stdin` and the checkpoint for the scaffold commit was never written. Upgrading Git for Windows to 2.55.0 fixed it: the next hook took 3 s and the checkpoint landed.
- **13:00 to 13:35 IST. Six worker agents built FirstRun in parallel** on main, one track each: fixtures, planner, executor, recovery, verify and output, report page. Each track is one commit with its own checkpoint.
- **13:35 IST. Layer 1 done.** `firstrun run https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/python` passed 4 of 4 steps in 70 s and wrote `report.md`. The first live run showed one run split into 3 neatlogs traces, so the CLI now opens one `firstrun.run` trace around reading, planning, every step and verification.

### v1 Runs, Layer 1 Only (Recovery Off), Tag `v1`

| Target | Result | Time | Cost (list price, not billed) |
|---|---|---|---|
| neatlogs Python SDK | passed 3/3 | 84 s | $0.036 |
| Entire CLI install | failed at step 1: `curl: command not found` on python:3.11-slim | n/a | $0.023 |
| Chroma getting started | passed 3/3 | 250 s | $0.029 |
| OpenAI v0 README (FIXTURE, Wayback 2023-08-02) | failed at step 6: `openai: command not found`, the documented CLI is gone from today's SDK | n/a | $0.031 |

neatlogs v1 traces, one `firstrun.run` trace per run, cost as neatlogs measured it:

| Target | Trace ID | Spans | Tool spans | LLM calls | neatlogs cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| neatlogs | `fccdbad9a9c6177b90112911fe485bd6` | 9 | 4 | 1 | $0.0397 |
| Entire | `10c44df9626c19f5ac801f1c6d84610e` | 7 | 2 | 1 | $0.0170 |
| Chroma | `66ec093b00333fa221fade5d2fc5f55f` | 9 | 4 | 1 | $0.0217 |
| OpenAI v0 FIXTURE | `b98b419e286acf436083febdb5217cf9` | 12 | 7 | 1 | $0.0266 |

Six mistakes the agent itself made in v1. These are the "before" story:

1. **The plan changes between runs.** The same neatlogs page gave 4 steps at 13:35 and 3 steps at 13:40.
2. **The planner invents steps.** It added `command -v entire`, `command -v git-remote-entire` and `test -f first_trace.py`, which are not in the docs.
3. **The planner writes placeholder steps.** Chroma step 2 is `true`, a no-op standing in for "create the file".
4. **A fake secret passes as a step.** The OpenAI step `export OPENAI_API_KEY='sk-...'` exits 0, so it counts as a pass while proving nothing.
5. **The planner skips the step that matters.** It dropped the OpenAI `openai.ChatCompletion.create` example and the neatlogs "run your app" step because they need a key. Those are the steps most likely to break.
6. **Most expected results check only the exit code.** 9 of 16 steps have no output check, so a command that prints an error and exits 0 would pass.

### Saturday Afternoon: neatlogs Found the Agent's Own Bug, and v2 Fixed It

- **14:10 IST.** Atharva created two neatlogs detections: "docs step broke" (TOOL spans) and "planner invented a step" (the planner span). The second flagged the planner spans of 3 v1 runs.
- **14:40 IST.** neatlogs Investigate (Deep, workflow `firstrun`) traced the invented steps to the planner prompt and proposed a stricter one ([evidence/neatlogs-investigation.md](evidence/neatlogs-investigation.md)).
- **14:45 IST.** A headless Claude Code session read the detection and its trend over the neatlogs MCP server and applied the fix with code guards and a plan cache: commit 3ca6f11, checkpoint `01M4JGJ6NTE7YNB9Z0YW5FYVHN`, [Entire commit view](https://entire.io/gh/HighnessAtharva/firstrun/commit/3ca6f118ecb0a8915315eea27b5588dd8a7c6299).
- **15:15 IST. v2 versus v1** on the same 4 targets: quickstarts finished 2 to 3 of 4, failed steps recovered 0 to 3, cost per run $0.0262 to $0.0200 (neatlogs). The v2 and real-world runs exposed 5 agent bugs, all fixed: a pipe that hid a missing `curl`, a multi-line step that hid a failing `pip`, pip noise that hid the real error, container fixes counted as docs bugs, and a file check after `cd`.

### Saturday Evening: Real Docs, Upstream PRs, and Entire Reviewing Every Layer

- **Real quickstarts:** dbt + DuckDB, AccuKnox knoxctl, Dagster, MkDocs and the Entire install all reached `verified` in a fresh container.
- **Upstream PRs, each from a verified run and a duplicate search:** [dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com#10149](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10149) (`jafgen --years` removed), [#10150](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10150) (Python 3.12 floor), [entireio/cli#2724](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2724) (Linux PATH after `install.sh`), [accuknox/help#671](https://github.com/accuknox/help/pull/671) (knoxctl page named 0.9.0 while the installer fetched 0.9.58).
- **No PR where the docs were right:** Dagster's page already covers both gaps FirstRun hit, so FirstRun opened nothing there. MkDocs needed only `curl` in the container.
- **Trails:** branch-backed Trails 3 to 8 cover every commit since kickoff. Entire runners raised 3 real bugs, all fixed and resolved with the commit SHA: a secret retry loop, a Windows-only Docker default, and a `cd` guard that was written but never called.
- **CI:** GitHub Actions runs the offline suite on every push. It caught 3 tests that passed only with a local Claude token.

### Saturday Night: Two New Answers From the Same Engine

- **Docs Bisect** (`firstrun bisect`): on the dbt guide, `jafgen --years 6` passes on jafgen 0.3.1 (2023-01-17) and fails on 0.4.6 (2024-04-07), and PyPI has no release between them. The guide merged on 2025-03-14, 11 months later. 5 probes, $0 in model calls. The evidence is a [comment on #10149](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10149#issuecomment-6096827074).
- **Prerequisite Proof** (`firstrun prereqs`): proven blocks for AccuKnox (curl, ca-certificates, gnupg, sudo, 5/5 steps), MkDocs (curl, 9/9 steps) and Entire (curl, git, `~/.local/bin` on PATH, 4/4 steps).
- **Website:** [1run.netlify.app](https://1run.netlify.app) takes a docs URL and writes a prompt for the visitor's own coding agent. A tested URL shows its cached run first. Every run prints a share link that replays read, plan, run, fix, prove, plus the bisect timeline and the assumptions card.
- **Jury self-test:** the Entire judge plugin ranked the repo with no excluded work, 3.93 of 5 ([evidence/jury-selftest.txt](evidence/jury-selftest.txt)).

### 2026-10-10, 17:45 to 18:05 IST: The Business Plan Sets the Agent's Budget

- **Done: `firstrun econ`.** The command reads 64 `firstrun.run` traces from neatlogs and writes [business/drivers.csv](business/drivers.csv) and [business/unit_economics.json](business/unit_economics.json). Mean cost per run is $0.0167, p95 is $0.0508 and max is $0.1014. Each quantile row names its trace ID.
- **Finding:** the fixed $0.50 cap in `models.py` was 30 times the mean run. If every run hit it, Scale margin would be -403.6%. At a 70% margin floor, the Scale cap is $0.028, and 25.0% of measured runs cost more than that. [business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md](business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md) gives two fixes from the same formula: Scale at $529, or Scale at 1,500 runs.
- **Done: `firstrun run --tier NAME`.** The executor and the recovery agent check the tier's cap in the `budget` GUARDRAIL span.
- **Live runs on the typer quickstart, tag `tiercap`:**
  - `--tier scale` ($0.0280 cap): verified 7/7 steps in 127 s with 8 patches, at $0.0201 list price. neatlogs trace `9a29db323b3d054bb2c82e82e080340f`.
  - `--tier free` ($0.0108 cap): stopped at step 4 with `cost budget spent`, after 4 patches and $0.0114. neatlogs trace `06e7f3765141c2f417a862beef5f5134`.
- **Tests:** 255 passed and 2 skipped in the offline suite, including 8 new tests in `tests/test_econ.py`.
  - `--tier free` again, after the cap message moved to 4 decimals: stopped at step 4 with `cost budget spent: $0.0115 of $0.0108`. neatlogs trace `7060f5bd8dbb8cdc6c1dec3830ba7bab`.
- **Known gap: two cost counters.** On 43 runs matched by start time, FirstRun's own count totals $1.5253 and neatlogs totals $1.0989, so FirstRun counts 39% higher. The gap holds after the traces finalized, so ingestion lag does not explain it. The cap checks FirstRun's count, so it stops a run early and never late. Unifying the two counters is next.
- **Done later the same evening:** Ari built the cfo.ai model from `drivers.csv` over the `cfoai` MCP server, with 6 Scenarios. It is public at [cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE](https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE).

### 2026-10-10, 18:30 to 19:30 IST: The Docs Execution Graph

- **Done:** `run.html` draws a graph from the docs page, through every step, to the fresh-container proof. A failed step branches into its container output, its proposed fix, its rerun and its evidence. Clicking a node opens a side panel with the quoted docs sentence, the command, the output, the change, and every attempt before and after.
- **Honest labels:** nodes read Passed, Failed as written, Blocked, Not run, or Not run: out of scope. Red means the docs are wrong. Amber means the container lacked a prerequisite and the docs were fine.
- **Evidence path:** a toggle shows neatlogs trace, Entire checkpoint, Entire session, Trail and PRs in order. The checkpoint and session pages open without a login. The Trail and the neatlogs trace need one, and the page says so. Entire Graph is not used, because it maps code, not docs steps.
- **Example:** the dbt replay links step 3 to [#10150](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10150) and step 10 to [#10149](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10149) and its bisect comment.
- **Fixes found while building it:** the share tail kept pip download lines and dropped the real error, so stderr now goes last. `report.md` called the step that ended a run its "First Failed Step" even after recovery fixed an earlier failure. It now names both steps, and the root span carries `reported_failed_step` for the neatlogs eval.
- **Checked:** desktop at 1280 px and phone at 375 px with no sideways scroll, the dbt, Dagster and fixture codes, and no console errors. Offline suite: 260 passed, 2 skipped.

### 2026-10-10, 19:00 IST: neatlogs Alerts, an AI Evaluator, and Public Proof Upstream

- **Alerts, created over the neatlogs CLI with write scopes Atharva approved:** "firstrun p95 run cost above Scale cap" (p95 `cost` above $0.035 over 1 day, `56b3b8be`), "firstrun docs breakage or failed verification spike" (compound rule on 2 detections, `74e5d64c`) and "firstrun budget guardrail tripped" (each Budget Limit Exceeded hit, `acd01964`). All three send email. A dry-run test of each returned `simulated` for email.
- **AI evaluator:** "report names the real failed step", an agent judge with neatlogs MCP access, a $0.10 budget and 12 tool calls (`a6aa683e`). An ad-hoc run returned `NOT_FOUND_OR_OPERATION_DISABLED` with gate `tier-c-compute`, so scoring runs only through a scheduled evaluation.
- **cfo.ai:** Ari built the model over the `cfoai` MCP from `drivers.csv`. Under the old $0.50 Scale cap, cash goes negative in month 14. The figures are in [business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md](business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md).
- **Public proof on the 4 upstream PRs:** each got a comment linking the live replay, opened on the fixed step, and the public Entire session. The comments are on [dbt #10149](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10149#issuecomment-6097945132), [dbt #10150](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10150#issuecomment-6097945350), [Entire #2724](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2724#issuecomment-6097945657) and [AccuKnox #671](https://github.com/accuknox/help/pull/671#issuecomment-6097945911).

List all connected social media accounts.

Use this to find account IDs needed for creating posts.

entries.name: mcp__zernio__analytics_get_best_time_to_post
entries.description:
Get best times to post

Returns the best times to post based on historical engagement data.
Groups all published posts by day of week and hour (UTC), calculating average engagement per slot.
Use this to auto-schedule posts at optimal times. Requires the Analytics add-on.

platform.description: Filter by platform (e.g. "instagram", "tiktok"). Omit for all platforms.

profile_id.description: Filter by profile ID. Omit for all profiles.

account_id.description: Filter by account ID. Omit for all accounts.

source.description: Filter by post origin. "late" for posts published via Zernio, "external" for posts imported from platforms.

Platform limits are sourced from each platform's actual upload constraints.

{"result":"Found 5 relevant section(s) for 'twitter X video duration limit 140 seconds':

--- Result 1: Long video uploads ---
## Long video uploads

`platformSpecificData.longVideo: true` uploads the video with X's `amplify_video` media category instead of the standard `tweet_video`. It is not what allows a long video: the standard path already publishes videos well past 140 seconds, on free accounts included. Zernio applies it only when the connected X account has a paid X subscription; on other accounts the flag is accepted and ignored. The maximum duration is set by X per account, not by Zernio, which enforces only the 512 MB file size. Some accounts also need X's long-video API allowlisting, without which X rejects an `amplify_video` upload.

---
name: write-linkedin-posts
description: Write, rewrite and ship LinkedIn posts for Atharva's personal profile as short list posts a stranger can use, in one of six winning templates, then run the checks, the card, the Zernio draft and the in-place Zernio update. Use when asked to write, refine, redo, review, schedule or batch LinkedIn content, fix weak Zernio LinkedIn drafts, or for any LinkedIn post, thought leadership piece or "make this a banger" request.
---

# LinkedIn Post Writer

Every post is a short list that solves one problem for a reader who has never heard of Atharva. Pick one of the six templates in `LIBRARY/Resources/LinkedIn Winning Templates 2026.md`, fill it with real facts, and run the checks. Decided 2026-10-09, after Depost's analysis of his last 19 posts.

## Pass the Stranger Test Before You Write

The reader does not know Atharva, his tools or his projects. Answer these four in writing before the first line.

1. **The reader.** Name one job title, such as "a founder shipping a developer tool".
2. **The pain.** Write the problem in the reader's words, in one sentence.
3. **The takeaway.** Write what the reader does in the next 10 minutes because of this post.
4. **The template.** Name it by number and name. Never use the template of the post scheduled just before this one.

If the pain only exists inside Atharva's own setup, the post fails. Find the reader's version of the problem, or drop the idea.

The insight must be box 4 in `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`: new to the reader, and usable today.

## Load These Files First

Read `DIGITAL TWIN/core/runtime-contract.md`, `DIGITAL TWIN/core/pattern-rules.md`, `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`, `DIGITAL TWIN/Voice.md`, the templates file, then this file. The banned words and punctuation are already in context from `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.

## Follow the Seven Rules in Every Post

1. **Open on the reader.** Line 1 names their problem or promises a list they can use. Never open on I, my, we, our, a product name or a tool name. `li_format.py` blocks this as `self-hook`.
2. **Make the list the post.** Use 3 to 9 items. Each item is a short name, then a `↳` line that says what it means for the reader. `li_format.py` blocks a post with fewer than 3 items as `no-list`.
3. **Explain every name.** A tool, product or term the reader may not know gets one plain line, or it goes. Jev, AgentZ, Magi, harness, vault and digital twin all need one.
4. **Keep only useful numbers.** A number stays when the reader can use it or a source is named. A number that only describes Atharva's own setup goes. Never invent a number.
5. **Put Atharva in once at most.** One line of proof is enough, such as "I tested this on 40 of my own posts."
6. **Keep it short.** The body runs 120 to 260 words. Each paragraph is 1 to 3 short lines.
7. **Close with use.** Write a one-line takeaway, then one specific question the reader can answer from their own work. Never "What do you think?"

No hashtags. No emoji in the body, except the 🌱 in the follow line. No jargon a reader must search for. No paragraph a reader must read twice.

## End Every Post With the Same Three Blocks

**1. The comment CTA,** directly above the follow line. One word in caps, and a real resource. Write the whole line in Unicode Mathematical Bold Sans-Serif, never Markdown `**`. The offsets are U+1D5D4 for A to Z, U+1D5EE for a to z, and U+1D7EC for 0 to 9.

𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 "𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗖𝗞" 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗜'𝗹𝗹 𝗗𝗠 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗽.

**2. The follow CTA,** exactly this line:

🌱 If you want to stay sharp on Product, AI, Technology, Marketing and content that helps you grow as a builder, click Follow. I publish consistently and keep it practical.

**3. The pinned comment,** after a `---` rule:

```
---
### 📌 PINNED COMMENT

{2 to 3 sentences of extra value}

→ {one URL}
```

The pinned comment carries one URL and no hashtag. If no URL exists, stop and ask Atharva for one.

Only one ask per post. A second plain `Comment "WORD"` line fails as `double-ask`.

## Use the Fixed File Shape

New posts go in `SOCIALS/LinkedIn/_WIP/<post-slug>/li_<Title>.md`. Check for an existing file on the topic first, and write into it rather than making a second one.

```markdown
---
type: LinkedIn Post
title: Caption Title
source_blog: "[[Exact Blog Title]]"
description: "The hook, one line"
created: YYYY-MM-DD
updated: YYYY-MM-DD
posted: false
---

[post starts here]
```

`source_blog` is the article title as a wikilink, or `none`. `media_asset:` and `media_alt:` are added by `groom.py`. Add no other field.

## Run the Checks Until Every CRIT Is Zero

```bash
python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"
python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py "<file>"
python SCRIPTS/socials/li_format.py "<file>"
python SCRIPTS/pillars/pillars.py "<file>"
```

Then read the post once as the stranger. If any line needs Atharva's context to make sense, rewrite it.

Render the load-order panel with `python SCRIPTS/loadorder/block.py --skill write-linkedin-posts --file "<path>" --node "<node>" --topic "<idea>" --format "T<n> <template name>" --insight "<box 4 insight>"`.

## Ship New Posts as Drafts and Fix Old Posts in Place

1. **Card.** Make it with the `social-cards` skill in `META/Attachments/li-images/<slug>/`, then run `python META/Attachments/li-images/_kit/groom.py <slug>`.
2. **Commit and push the media first.** Zernio keeps an upload for 7 days, and the repo is the copy that lasts.
3. **New post.** `python SCRIPTS/zernio/li_draft.py "<file>"` is the dry run. Add `--live` to save the Zernio draft.
4. **Changed post that Zernio already holds.** `python SCRIPTS/zernio/li_update.py "<file>"` is the dry run. Add `--live` to replace the text and the first comment in place. It keeps the date, the image and the status, and it refuses a post that is already published. Never delete and recreate a scheduled post.
5. **Schedule.** `python SCRIPTS/zernio/li_schedule.py`. Monday to Friday, 5 posts a week at most, 10:00 AM US Eastern.
6. **Close the session.** Rebuild the desk with `python SCRIPTS/review/build.py`, then commit and push.

`references/pipeline.md` covers the batch review, the patch tool and post day. A batch of 5 or more gets the fresh-agent review in `references/icp-review-brief.md`.

## References

- `LIBRARY/Resources/LinkedIn Winning Templates 2026.md`: the six templates, the Depost numbers and the three benchmark posts.
- `references/examples.md`: rewritten posts that pass every check, one per template.
- `references/pipeline.md`: the stages after the draft.
- `references/icp-review-brief.md` and `references/patch-brief.md`: the batch review and batch fix briefs.
- The retired skill, hook library and example bank sit in `ARCHIVE/write-linkedin-posts retired 2026-10-09/`.
